newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Korean car makers target Russian market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Korean car makers target Russian market.

text.p: South Korea's ambitious car makers, powered by what they say is a winning combination of price and quality, are speeding into Russia's huge market.
"You just can't compare Korean cars with Russian ones due to the low quality of the latter, while Western cars are more expensive," Daewoo Corp Moscow manager Sang-Yeon Lee said.
"If you ask about our strategy in Russia, we are very active and very aggressive," Lee told Reuters.
Daewoo took part in the 4th Moscow International Motor Show last month alongside other leading world car makers.
This year's show was dedicated to the 100th anniversary of Russia's car industry, but Korean producers say 1996 could be a successful turning point in their sales in Russia, and some Russians agree.

"In general, Korean cars have a bright future in Russia. They are of very good quality and inexpensive and, therefore, preferable for us to European ones," said Yevgeny Levichev, an official from Russia's ASM-Holding, and one of the organisers of the show.
Last year Daewoo sold around 3,000 cars in Russia and plans to boost this figure to more than 8,000 this year. Sales are expected to rise by over 50 percent in 1997, Lee said.
The Nexia sedan, on display at the motor show, accounts for over 70 percent of Daewoo sales here.
Daewoo will assemble jointly with Russia's Krasny Aksai some 4,000 to 5,000 of its popular Nexia and Espero sedans this year in the southern Russian city of Rostov.
"You can buy a Nexia in Moscow for some $15,000-16,000, but we expect to bring the price down next year when assembly volumes in Rostov pick up," Lee said.
KIA Motors is another company which intends to drive down the local cost of its cars by investing in plant in Russia.
KIA plans to invest a total of $1.2 billion over five years in a car plant in Russia's western enclave of Kaliningrad, including $180 million to be put in by the end of this year.

KIA and its Russian partner, the Kaliningrad-based Yantar shipbuilding company, plan to start assembling Korean cars by the end of this year, raising output to 55,000 cars in 1997 and 120,000 by the year 2,000.
Denis Titov, sales expert at LG International Corp, the official importer of KIA cars in Russia -- said cars assembled in Kaliningrad would be some 30 percent cheaper than now.
KIA hopes to find a place on the Russian market for its Sephia sedans and Sportage jeeps.

"KIA cars will be popular among Russians, because their future price of $13,000 to $20,000 is close to the price of Russian cars," Titov said, adding LG expects to sell more than 7,000 cars next year, compared to 3,000 in 1996.
The latest Zhiguli VAZ 2110 sedan offered by Russia's AvtoVAZ car maker retails for 73-74 million roubles (about $14,000).
Hyundai, another Korean car maker, also plans to push down the price of its cars to make them more attractive to Russians.
The company sold more than 3,500 cars in Russia in 1995 and plans to increase this figure to some 5,500 this year.

"Russia is a promising market for us, although Hyundai is not as well known here as Ford or Mercedes... But we believe Hyundai's worldwide fame will start on Russia's huge and promising market," said Weon-Woo Seo, deputy manager of the automobile division of Hyundai's CIS team.
"If you need my personal viewpoint, it would be better to assemble our cars in Russia to beat their prices down, but it is up to my chiefs to decide," Seo said.
SsangYong Corporation is another Korean car maker unworried that its name is largely unknown to most Russians.
"Russia has very bad roads and severe winters, so this is very good for our Musso jeeps," said Jin-Shug Lee, the company's Moscow representative.
The company expects sales of its jeeps, which cost $35,000 to $37,000 in Moscow, to rise next year to 1,000 from some 600 this year.
"But like other Korean producers SsangYong might also wish to set up a car assembly in Russia, so these sales forecasts would seem too marginal then," Lee said.
